limitations: The allowlist contains a duplicated entry, PBEWithHmacSHA384AndAES_128; duplication has no apparent set-membership effect.
The rule does not define speccedKey; its meaning and producers must be established from other rules or detector documentation.
The rule has no explicit constraint on the provider argument represented by _.

detector_semantics.claim: The rule accepts the declared protocol only when a Get event precedes a Gen event, the Get event's algorithm satisfies the explicit CRYSL membership constraint, and a generateSecret event has a keySpec carrying the required speccedKey[keySpec, _] predicate. It then provides generatedKey[key, algorithm] as an ensured detector fact.

documented_behavior: javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory is a factory for secret (symmetric) keys and converts between secret-key objects and transparent key specifications.

getInstance(String) returns a SecretKeyFactory for the requested algorithm by selecting the first registered provider that supports it; the overloads with a provider name or Provider object select that provider.
generateSecret(KeySpec) generates a SecretKey from supplied key-specification material.
translateKey(SecretKey) translates a key whose provider may be unknown or untrusted into a corresponding key object of this factory.
preconditions: For getInstance, algorithm must not be null; a supporting provider must exist, and provider-specific overloads additionally require a valid provider name or Provider object.
For generateSecret, the supplied KeySpec must be appropriate for the selected SecretKeyFactory or InvalidKeySpecException is thrown.
For translateKey, the supplied SecretKey must be processable by the selected SecretKeyFactory or InvalidKeyException is thrown.
unknowns: The official API documentation does not define the detector-specific predicate speccedKey[keySpec, _].
The official API documentation does not state that every rule-allowlisted algorithm is implemented by every Java runtime, Android runtime, or third-party provider.
The documented API alone does not determine whether a particular provider accepts aliases such as provider-specific PBE names.
The API documentation does not specify whether the detector recognizes all source-level forms of the calls, including static imports, wrappers, reflection, or indirect dispatch.

important_note: This is a detector policy over selected javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory call traces and algorithm-name values. It does not prove that a call succeeds, that a derived or translated key is cryptographically secure, that the provider supports the requested algorithm, or that a rejected algorithm is unsuitable for a particular compatibility requirement.
forbidden_inferences_without_evidence: Do not infer that a listed algorithm is available from the selected or default security provider.
Do not infer that getInstance, generateSecret, or translateKey completed successfully; each documented API can throw an exception.
Do not infer PBKDF2 salt quality, iteration count, password entropy, derived-key length, or output-key use from this rule.
Do not infer that a translated key was derived with PBKDF2 or with any password-based construction.
Do not infer that an algorithm excluded from the rule is necessarily insecure or inappropriate; the rule is an allowlist policy, not a complete compatibility or security analysis.
Do not infer that a provider alias, an alternate spelling, or an algorithm name accepted at runtime will be recognized by the detector's literal constraint.
Do not infer that generatedKey[key, algorithm] means the key material is extractable, persistent, approved by a compliance regime, or safe for a particular cipher mode or protocol.

security_semantics.runtime_claim: At runtime, a factory may be created only if the requested algorithm and provider are supported; generating or translating a key succeeds only if the provider can process the supplied object. Actual security depends on provider behavior and parameters not constrained by this rule.
security_semantics.detector_claim: A matching call trace uses an algorithm name from the rule's restricted list, follows Get before Gen, and—when generateSecret is used—has the detector's required key-spec predicate.

compatibility: Identify stored-data, protocol, or peer-interoperability requirements before changing an algorithm name.
Verify the exact provider and platform support for the requested SecretKeyFactory algorithm and any aliases.
For PBKDF2 or PBE use, verify the complete parameter format and derivation/encryption behavior needed to read existing data or interoperate with other implementations.
runtime: Observe the actual algorithm string supplied when getInstance executes.
Observe provider selection, provider registration, and provider support for the requested algorithm.
Observe whether getInstance, generateSecret, or translateKey returns normally rather than throwing.
For generateSecret, inspect the runtime KeySpec and its provider-specific compatibility with the selected factory.
source_level: Resolve the invoked method to javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory rather than a namesake API.
Establish which getInstance overload is invoked and trace the algorithm argument to a concrete value or a bounded set of values.
Establish the relevant call order between the factory acquisition and generateSecret or translateKey on the tracked factory object.
For generateSecret, identify evidence that produces or establishes speccedKey[keySpec, _] in the detector's rule ecosystem.

name: SecretKeyFactorySpec
semantic_scope: For every finding of this rule, the detector is concerned with calls resolved to javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory that form the declared Get-then-Gen protocol: either getInstance(algorithm) or getInstance(algorithm, _) followed by either generateSecret(keySpec) or translateKey(otherKey). It constrains the algorithm value associated with the getInstance event to the rule's explicit allowlist and, for generateSecret, requires the detector predicate speccedKey[keySpec, _]. It does not observe calls to unrelated classes merely because their names end in Spec, and it does not make getKeySpec an event in this protocol.
known_false_positive_shapes: A runtime-supported provider alias or non-standard algorithm spelling is rejected because it is absent from the rule's explicit list.
An application must retain an excluded algorithm name to read legacy data or interoperate with an external system, even though the rule reports the name.
The algorithm value is computed, loaded from configuration, or passed through an unanalyzed wrapper, so static analysis cannot prove its membership in the allowlist.
The call is on an unreachable, disabled, test-only, or exception-only path, but static analysis still reports the syntactic or feasible abstract path.

A standard name is supplied using a capitalization or normalization that the runtime accepts but the detector's value analysis does not normalize; Java's standard-name specification says standard names are not case-sensitive, while this rule expresses a finite set of capitalized string literals.
A valid generateSecret call is reported because the analysis cannot establish the undocumented detector predicate speccedKey[keySpec, _], despite runtime KeySpec compatibility.
protocol: Get, Gen where Get := g1 | g2 and Gen := gS | tK

policy.scope: This authorization applies when the derived bytes are stored and later recomputed from the user's secret to verify it (a PIN, password or passphrase hash), or are a key derived from that secret that protects data the app stores itself. It does not apply to a value another system computes or expects.
authorization_conditions: The examined scope shows the derived value is stored and verified by recomputing it from the user's input, or is a key that encrypts data the app stores itself.
No server, protocol or other application computes or expects the same value.
policy.strategy: Verify, then migrate. Keep the current derivation, unchanged, as the legacy path: a stored value produced the old way is still verified with exactly the old parameters. When that verification succeeds, derive a new value from the same user input with compliant parameters and store it together with a marker of how it was derived (a version or the parameters), so later checks use the new derivation; values created from now on always use the compliant parameters. If the derived bytes are an encryption key for stored data, decrypt with the old key and re-encrypt under the new key in the same step, after the old key opened the data. Choose the compliant parameters as named constants (for example PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 with an iteration count well above the rule's minimum), never from a value a caller passes.

required_numeric_constants.purpose: Named iteration count for newly created verifiers, above the detector minimum. Measure unlock latency on supported Android devices. Keep the legacy count unchanged for legacy verification only.

policy.finding_semantics: The violation is real: the stored verifier is weaker than the rule admits. Existing users must keep working, which is why the old derivation stays for verification only.
forbidden_changes: Do not change the existing derivation in place: a stored value produced the old way would stop verifying and the user would be locked out.
Do not remove the legacy verification while values in the old form may exist.
Do not lower a parameter or choose the new parameters from a caller-supplied value.
Do not change what is stored without a marker that tells the old form from the new one.
required_tests: A value stored with the old derivation still verifies with the correct input and is then stored in the new form.
A value stored in the new form verifies with the correct input.
A wrong input fails for both forms.
policy.review_fallback: Generate MULTI_FILE_FIX_PROPOSED_FOR_REVIEW when the verify-then-migrate path is complete but how the stored value is located or rewritten could not be confirmed in the examined scope.
